content: The study protocol for a cluster-randomized trial on HIV combination prevention interventions, including universal testing and treatment, was published in Trials in 2014. Chamie et al. (2014) reported on the uptake of community-based HIV testing during a multi-disease health campaign in rural Uganda, as published in PLoS One. Jain et al. (2014) described the successful delivery of antiretroviral therapy (ART) and retention in care among asymptomatic individuals with high CD4+ T-cell counts (>350 cells/μL) in rural Uganda, as detailed in AIDS. The World Health Organization (WHO) updated its 2010 antiretroviral guidelines in 2012 to include lifelong ART (Option B+) as a recommended approach to prevent mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) of HIV. Option B+ involves initiating ART at diagnosis and continuing for life, while Option B involves ART during pregnancy and breastfeeding only. The rapid adoption of Option B+ raised concerns about implementation challenges and the lack of validated benefits. The objective of the systematic review was to assess the effectiveness of lifelong ART (Option B+) compared to ART limited to pregnancy and breastfeeding (Option B) in pregnant and breastfeeding women living with HIV. The review used Cochrane Collaboration methods to search for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and cohort studies comparing the two interventions. However, due to limited data, a non-comparative review of studies on Options B and B+ was conducted. Primary outcomes of interest included maternal mortality, morbidity, adverse events, adherence, mother-to-child transmission, HIV transmission to sexual partners, development of antiretroviral resistance, retention in treatment, ART discontinuation and re-initiation (Option B), tuberculosis incidence, fertility rate, maternal CD4 count, and viral load. Secondary outcomes included the sustainability of service delivery and patient acceptability. The review identified 525 studies for screening, but no RCTs or observational studies directly comparing Option B+ to Option B met the inclusion criteria. Instead, 16 studies on Option B and 13 on Option B+ were included for narrative synthesis. These studies, conducted in various countries including sub-Saharan Africa, investigated outcomes such as maternal mortality, ART adherence, mother-to-child transmission, retention in treatment, maternal CD4 count, viral load, and patient acceptability. The analysis highlighted suboptimal retention and poor adherence to treatment under Option B+, suggesting the need for improved implementation strategies. Enhanced patient counseling and robust infant follow-up were recommended to address gaps in the PMTCT cascade. The WHO's 2013 Consolidated ART Guidelines reiterated the recommendation for a once-daily fixed-dose combination regimen for adults, including pregnant and breastfeeding women, with tenofovir (TDF), efavirenz (EFV), and either lamivudine (3TC) or emtricitabine (FTC). Option B+ offers several advantages, including simplified regimens, safety for mothers and infants, reduced tuberculosis risk, lower monitoring requirements, and prevention of sexual transmission. However, concerns about implementation challenges and the lack of validated benefits remain. The review concluded that while Option B+ shows promise in reducing maternal mortality and improving virological suppression, retention in care and adherence remain significant challenges. Further research and improved implementation strategies are necessary to optimize outcomes for women and children affected by HIV.
